summary: Requires that TLS clients and servers never negotiate SSL version 2.0, because it is known to be insecure. It updates the backward compatibility sections of RFC 2246, RFC 4346 and RFC 5246. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: SSL 2.0 is an old secret lock with known flaws. This says computers must refuse to use it.

subtitle: Requires TLS clients and servers never to negotiate the insecure SSL version 2.0.

tldr.problem: Some TLS clients and servers still supported negotiating SSL version 2.0, which has known deficiencies and does not give a sufficiently high level of security.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC updates the backward compatibility sections of TLS 1.0, 1.1 and 1.2: clients MUST NOT send an SSL 2.0 compatible CLIENT-HELLO and servers MUST NOT reply with an SSL 2.0 SERVER-HELLO.
tldr.outcome: SSL 2.0 may never be negotiated. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists RFC 8996 as updating it.

today: RFC 6176 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2246, RFC 4346 and RFC 5246, and RFC 8996 is listed as updating it.

sections.title: Why SSL 2.0 Goes
sections.content:
Many IETF protocols rely on TLS, but some TLS clients and servers also support negotiating SSL version 2.0, which has known deficiencies. This document requires that TLS clients and servers never negotiate it.

RFC 4346 and later RFC 5246 had warned that the ability to send version 2.0 CLIENT-HELLO messages "will be phased out with all due haste". RFC 6176 does this by updating the backward compatibility sections of RFC 2246, RFC 4346 and RFC 5246.
sections.plainLanguage: Earlier rule books said to stop using the old lock soon. This one says stop now.

sections.title: The SSL 2.0 Deficiencies
sections.content:
The RFC lists four problems:

  • Message authentication uses MD5.
  • Handshake messages are not protected, so a man-in-the-middle can trick the client into picking a weaker cipher suite.
  • Message integrity and message encryption use the same key, which is a problem if a weak algorithm is negotiated.
  • Sessions can easily be terminated: a man-in-the-middle can insert a TCP FIN, and the peer cannot tell whether it was a legitimate end of the session.
sections.plainLanguage: The old lock used a weak seal, let a sneaky person change the deal before it started, used one key for two jobs, and could be slammed shut by a stranger.

sections.title: What TLS Implementations Must Do
sections.content:
TLS clients MUST NOT send the SSL version 2.0 compatible CLIENT-HELLO format, and MUST NOT send any ClientHello specifying a protocol version less than { 0x03, 0x00 }. A client SHOULD specify the highest protocol version it supports.

TLS servers MAY continue to accept ClientHello messages in the version 2 CLIENT-HELLO format from RFC 5246, Appendix E.2, which does not contradict the ban on negotiating SSL 2.0. Servers MUST NOT reply with an SSL 2.0 SERVER-HELLO below { 0x03, 0x00 } and MUST abort the connection, so a client whose highest version is { 0x02, 0x00 } is refused.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients must not ask for the old lock. If a client only knows the old lock, the server hangs up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that the entire document is about security considerations. It adds that the number of servers supporting the optional acceptance of the version 2 CLIENT-HELLO is declining, and that this hello format precludes TLS extensions, which can only be sent in an (Extended) ClientHello handshake message.
sections.plainLanguage: The old greeting also cannot carry the newer safety add-ons.
